profile.reading:
DataBank's Silicon Valley facility, SFO1, sits at 5101 Lafayette Street, Santa Clara, California. DataBank's own facility page states 16,680 square feet of IT space and 3 megawatts of critical IT load, built to an N+1 power and N+1 cooling design supporting 10 kilowatt-plus rack densities, with 4 onsite network carriers and SOC 1/2, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 compliance certifications. DataBank does not name the power utility on SFO1's page; Silicon Valley Power, the City of Santa Clara's municipal electric utility, serves much of Santa Clara including its dense data center corridor, though this is not stated by DataBank directly. DataBank's own acquisition-history page, which lists the company's growth through purchases of C7 Data Centers, 365 Data Centers, Lightbound, Zayo's zColo business, and CyrusOne Houston assets, does not mention a Santa Clara or Silicon Valley acquisition, implying SFO1 was built or opened organically by DataBank rather than acquired, though DataBank does not state this explicitly or give a year. Santa Clara sits at the center of one of the most supply-constrained data center markets in the country; Silicon Valley Power has at times paused new large-load interconnection requests while it builds additional substation capacity, a constraint that has pushed some hyperscale and colocation growth toward Santa Clara's edges and neighboring cities. DataBank's Santa Clara presence sits among a dense cluster of competing operators, including Digital Realty, Equinix, CoreSite, and Vantage facilities within a few miles of SFO1.

Silicon Valley Power's municipal ownership structure, unlike investor-owned utilities such as PG&E serving most of the rest of the Bay Area, gives the City of Santa Clara direct control over industrial power allocation policy, a dynamic that has periodically shaped which new data center projects can secure timely interconnection in the city. California's Title 24 building energy-efficiency code and statewide water-efficiency standards shape cooling-system design requirements for all new Silicon Valley data center construction, including any future expansion DataBank might pursue at or near SFO1.

[process narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is attributed in the registry to DataBank. DataBank Ltd. was established in 2005 in a historic former Federal Reserve Bank building in downtown Dallas, Texas, that had been converted to a data center in 1999, per DataBank own corporate history page fetched this session. DataBank was acquired in July 2016 by a group of investors led by DigitalBridge, per that same page. DataBank own history page also lists a series of acquisitions expanding its footprint, three Salt Lake City area data centers from C7 Data Centers plus facilities in Cleveland and Pittsburgh from 365 Data Centers in January 2017, Lightbound, an Indianapolis based provider, in December 2018, United States and United Kingdom data center assets from zColo in December 2020, and four Houston area data centers from CyrusOne for 670 million dollars in January 2022. A trade press article fetched this session, from pe-insights.com, reports that DigitalBridge agreed to sell a 27 percent fully diluted equity stake in DataBank to Swiss Life Asset Management and EDF Invest for about 1.2 billion dollars, expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2022, reducing DigitalBridge own stake to about 15.5 percent and yielding DigitalBridge about 230 million dollars in cash proceeds. DataBank own history page states the company now operates more than 65 data centers across more than 27 markets. The operator own dedicated page for this facility, Santa Clara SFO1, fetched this session, confirms the address already on file, 5101 Lafayette Street, Santa Clara, CA 95054, and states 3 MW of critical IT load and 16,680 IT square feet.

reading.body:
DataBank SFO1 publishes 3 MW of IT capacity across 16,680 square feet of technical space at 5101 Lafayette Street in Santa Clara. At 10 kW per rack, a common colocation density, 3 MW supports roughly 300 racks; at 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, the same load supports roughly 75 racks. The operator has not published a per-rack power envelope, so neither figure is an operator claim. The footprint and power together suggest a mid-sized colocation building rather than a hyperscale campus.

No certifications appear in the published specifications, so no statement can be made about which workload tiers or compliance regimes the facility qualifies to host. Uptime rating, SOC attestations, and similar credentials are not published on the page this site read.

Among the 103 facilities mapped in California, only 5 have published a megawatt figure, and those 5 account for 170 MW in total on this site's records. SFO1 ranks fifth among those five by published IT capacity, contributing 3 of the 170 MW, or roughly 1.8 percent of the published California total this site holds. That position reflects the limits of what operators choose to publish as much as it reflects the campus's actual scale; 98 of the 103 mapped California facilities publish no capacity figure at all.
